blocks: Every faithful option is AGPL-3.0, and Looksyk is AGPL-3.0 too. The permissively licensed neighbor, markdown-oxide (Apache-2.0), is built around Obsidian vaults and its README does not mention Logseq. So garden-core will be AGPL-3.0 unless it writes its own parser, and the Brief's licensing bullet can be resolved today.

Tine is a Logseq-compatible outliner that reads and writes the same pages/, journals/, assets/, and logseq/config.edn as Logseq, with a pure-Rust core and an in-memory cache for search, backlinks, and queries. It ships static HTML export with offline search and a native Android build. It was created in late June 2026 and was last pushed today.
Pick the parser first and let the language follow

That is most of the "fast, faithful, local semantic engine" the Brief describes, already written, three months old, by one maintainer. My/Principle/Simplify/Fewer and Deeper says to use a credible abstraction layer instead of building the component again. My/Pref/Dev/Tool/Prefer Well-Maintained Projects asks for a credible maintainer and healthy maintenance together; here maintenance is very healthy and the maintainer is new and alone, which that page calls a decision point.

Run lsdoc's own differential harness against the encode garden. lsdoc reports exact matches, classified intentional deviations, and unclassified mismatches against real mldoc. Zero unclassified mismatches on the encode garden means lsdoc is faithful for this corpus and the Rust path is open with the parser already done.
Pick the parser first and let the language follow

If lsdoc passes, build garden-core in Rust on lsdoc, and open an issue on Tine proposing that a CLI and an LSP share tine-core. Whether garden-core ends up as a crate beside tine-core or as a client of it is a conversation to have with the maintainer, and it would give Tine a second contributor.
Pick the parser first and let the language follow

If lsdoc fails on constructs the encode garden uses, build on mldoc in OCaml. Logseq is rewriting core pieces in OCaml: datascript-ocaml, a persistent sorted set, an FSRS library, and the official Logseq CLI are all OCaml. That CLI compiles to JavaScript through Melange, targets DB graphs only, and runs a db-worker-node server with a lock file and a random port, which is the operational shape the Brief rules out. It is prior art for command vocabulary and for a .mli-first spec style, and it is a reason to expect mldoc to stay maintained.

The order is right. This page argues for making the first shipped client the CLI that agents use in this repository, and for measuring the project by whether those agents stop grepping.

Every agent session in this garden checks whether a page exists by grepping pages/ and journals/. The repository's own instructions say to, and the link-hygiene skill exists because agents invent wikilinks when the grep is skipped. That is the Brief's "agents should not need to independently rediscover Logseq semantics by grepping a graph" problem, and it happens here several times a day.

Agents calling the CLI justify a persistent cache on a small garden

My Person/codekiln/GitHub/logseq-gardener/Analysis/Fable/26/09/12/0658 ET Measure the corpus before designing the cache argued for an in-memory index and file watching first, with the persistent cache added only when a cold parse gets long enough to notice. Codex's Person/codekiln/GitHub/logseq-gardener/Analysis/Codex/26/09/12/0733 ET Benchmark repeated commands and edits to widely linked pages points at the case that argument skipped: an agent runs the CLI as a fresh process for every lookup, so it pays the cold parse every time. On the hub page codekiln added that Looksyk and Tine have both had performance problems and that frontier performance is the interest. Together those change my recommendation.
Agents calling the CLI justify a persistent cache on a small garden
An agent pays the cold parse on every call
Agents calling the CLI justify a persistent cache on a small garden

An agent session in this repository checks pages many times: the link-hygiene skill resolves every wikilink in a draft, and the core rule says to grep before linking. If each garden page resolve costs a one-second cold parse, a session spends minutes waiting and the agent goes back to grep, which is the outcome this project exists to end. A persistent index turns each of those calls into a file open and a lookup.
Agents calling the CLI justify a persistent cache on a small garden

So the persistent cache belongs in the first release that agents use, whatever the encode garden's cold-parse time turns out to be. I would still run the benchmark first, and read its numbers to pick the cache format, the invalidation rule, and the latency targets.

Agents calling the CLI justify a persistent cache on a small garden

One SQLite file per checkout, under the XDG cache directory, holding pages, blocks, references, aliases, and a content hash for every source file. A command opens the file, compares each source file's size and modification time with the recorded ones the way git status does, rehashes only the files that changed, reparses those, and then re-resolves the links whose targets those files could have changed. Git's index has used the size-and-mtime shortcut for decades, so it is a known quantity.
Agents calling the CLI justify a persistent cache on a small garden

The re-resolving step is the one codekiln called pretentious when Codex first named it, so here it is plainly. After an edit the engine does two jobs: it re-reads the file that changed, and it re-checks links in other files whose target that change may have moved. 588fb79e docs: point nvim/Distro/LazyVim at LazyVim page removed alias:: [[nvim/Distro/LazyVim]] from the LazyVim page, and every [[nvim/Distro/LazyVim]] link in this garden changed target in a commit that edited none of the files holding those links. A lookup from each name to the blocks that reference it makes the second job a list walk.
